description: What helps people feel that they truly belong—and what happens when they do? Join the UCSF Climate and Belonging's Fostering Awareness Speaker Series on October 28th from 12:10–1:00 p.m. for The Science of Belonging, featuring UCSF’s Mica Estrada, PhD. Part of the Fostering Awareness: Dimensions of Belonging series, this session will explore the research behind belonging and the ways our environments, relationships, and everyday interactions can influence whether people feel valued, connected, and able to thrive. Dr. Estrada is Associate Dean of Opportunity & Engagement and Professor in the UCSF School of Nursing. Her research examines social influence, identity, values, kindness, well-being, mentorship, and approaches that strengthen inclusion and persistence in STEMM communities. Register for Zoom through the link provided below: https://ucsf.zoom.us/webinar/register/WN_VmsyEODgSouO-U3yTktoGg UCSF endeavors to create greater understanding and supports the exchange of diverse ideas. description: Exercise can improve physical functioning in cancer patients. It can reduce the feelings of fatigue, depression, nausea and weakness that can arise during and after cancer treatment. The UCSF Core and More class includes Pilates-based mat exercises to work on core strength and stability. We use rollers, bands and body weight as tools to enhance range of motion, flexibility, balance and muscular strength. Our goal is for you to have fun and increase your ability to perform daily activities. This class is sponsored by the UCSF Cancer Resource Center. It is open to current UCSF cancer patients and survivors. Registration is required for this class. To participate, you must undergo a pre-screening with an exercise counselor. For more information, call (415) 502-5547. There may be a waitlist for this course.

description: Presented by: Dr. Jessica Allanson, Licensed Clinical Psychologist, UCSF Faculty and Staff Assistance Program Artificial intelligence is becoming an increasingly present part of our everyday lives. From helping us organize information and brainstorm ideas to offering advice, companionship, or even support during difficult moments, AI tools are changing not only how we work, but also how we seek information, make decisions, and relate to technology. As these tools become more sophisticated and more human-like in their interactions, it is increasingly important to consider what their use may mean for our mental health and wellbeing. What does it look like to engage with AI in a way that supports rather than undermines our wellbeing? When might AI be helpful, and when should we be cautious? How can we recognize when our own (or someone else’s) relationship with AI may be becoming concerning? Join us for a 1-hour informational webinar exploring AI use through a mental health lens. Drawing from current research and psychological perspectives, we will discuss both the potential benefits and risks of engaging with AI and consider practical ways to use these rapidly evolving tools safely and intentionally. This webinar will focus on: Reviewing current research on AI use and mental healthExploring potential mental health benefits of AI when used appropriatelyUnderstanding psychological risks and concerns associated with AI useIdentifying signs that our own or someone else's relationship with AI may warrant greater attentionDiscussing practical steps for establishing healthy boundaries and supporting safer, more intentional AI useAI is likely to remain an evolving part of our personal and professional lives. Developing a healthy relationship with these tools does not require avoiding them altogether. It begins with understanding how they can affect us, recognizing where their limitations matter, and making thoughtful choices about when and how we engage. Please note: This webinar approaches AI from a mental health and psychological wellbeing perspective. It is not intended to provide information technology, cybersecurity, data privacy, or UCSF-specific AI policy guidance. Bio: Jessica Allanson, PhD, MA, is a licensed clinical psychologist with the Faculty and Staff Assistance Program at UCSF and runs the FSAP Post-Doctoral Fellowship Program. Dr. Allanson has chosen to specialize in recovery from substance use and workplace burnout, working primarily with those in high-intensity work settings and with high-achieving populations. She incorporates empirically-validated skill-based learning as well as industrial/organizational psychology strategies into her work with individual clients, teams, leaders, and learners. Dr. Allanson believes in the power of compassionate education and hopes to use her passion for sharing and teaching to support and empower those who are curious., powered by Localist, the Community Event Platform
